sections.h2: What is an estoppel certificate when you sell a Florida condo or HOA home?
sections.html:
An estoppel certificate is the association's written statement of what you owe and what fees apply to your unit or lot as of a given date. The buyer's lender and the title agent rely on it to set the payoff at closing. Condominium associations issue it under section 718.116(8) of the Florida Statutes, and homeowners' associations issue it under section 720.30851.

Request it as soon as you have a signed contract. The association must name on its website a person or entity, with a street or email address, to receive requests, so start there.

sections.h2: How fast must the association deliver it?
sections.html:
Within 10 business days after it receives a written or electronic request from the owner, the owner's designee, or the mortgagee. It must be delivered by hand, regular mail or email on the day it is issued. If the association misses the 10 business days, it cannot charge a fee for that certificate.

A summary court proceeding under section 51.011 can compel compliance, and the winning side recovers reasonable attorney fees. Most sellers never need that, but it shows the weight the statute puts on the deadline.

  • Effective period: 30 days if hand delivered or emailed, 35 days if sent by regular mail.
  • Amended certificate: free of charge if new information or a mistake surfaces in that period, and it starts a new 30 or 35 days.
  • Reliance: the association gives up the right to collect amounts above those stated from anyone who relies on the certificate in good faith.

sections.h2: What can the association charge for it?
sections.html:
The statute caps the fee at $250 when no delinquent amounts are owed on the unit. A request delivered within 3 business days on an expedited basis may add $100. If money is owed to the association, the added fee may not exceed $150. The statute also says the fee authority must come from a written board resolution or a written management contract.

The caps adjust every five years by the Consumer Price Index, and the Department of Business and Professional Regulation publishes the adjusted amounts on its website, so check there before you pay. If the closing falls through and the payer who is not the owner asks within 30 days after the closing date, the fee is refunded within 30 days of the request, and the owner is responsible for the refund.

sections.h2: What does the certificate have to list?
sections.html:
It lists the regular assessment and how often it is paid, the date it is paid through, and the next installment due. It must include an itemized list of all assessments, special assessments and other money owed, plus items scheduled to come due during the effective period.

Other questions the form asks are useful to a seller before the buyer sees them.

  • Is a capital contribution, resale or transfer fee due, and how much?
  • Is any rule violation open and noticed to the owner?
  • Does the board need to approve the transfer, and has it?
  • Is there a right of first refusal for members or the association, and has it been exercised?
  • Which other associations is the unit a member of, and who insures the association?

The condominium form adds a line for a parking or garage space number and, where the account went to collections, the name and contact information of the attorney, which the association cannot charge for.

sections.h2: Do unpaid assessments follow the unit to the buyer?
sections.html:
Yes, to a degree. Under section 718.116(1), a new unit owner is jointly and severally liable with the previous owner for unpaid assessments that came due before transfer. The new owner may recover from the seller, and the person acquiring title must pay the amount owed to the association within 30 days after the transfer.

Unpaid assessments bear interest at the rate in the declaration, or 18 percent a year if the declaration is silent. If the declaration allows it, the association may add a late fee of up to the greater of $25 or 5 percent of the late installment. Payments go first to interest, then late fees, then collection costs and attorney fees, then the assessment itself.

An association also holds a lien on the condominium parcel. A claim of lien stops being effective one year after recording unless the association starts a suit, and an owner can record a notice of contest that gives the association 90 days to sue. Pay off the figure on the estoppel at closing so the title agent can obtain a lien release.

sections.h2: What must a condo seller hand the buyer?
sections.html:
At the seller's expense, the buyer is entitled to a current copy of the declaration, the articles of incorporation, the bylaws and rules, the annual financial statement and budget, and the Frequently Asked Questions and Answers document. Section 718.503(2) also lists the inspector-prepared summary of any milestone inspection report and the most recent structural integrity reserve study, or a statement that none has been completed.

A resale contract must carry one of two clauses in conspicuous type. One says the buyer got the documents more than 7 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, before signing. The other makes the agreement voidable by written notice within 7 such days after signing and receipt of the documents. A contract that leaves out the required wording can be voided by the buyer before closing.

sections.h2: Why do reserves and structural studies matter to a sale?
sections.html:
A buyer's lender and the buyer will read the budget, and under section 718.112 the budget must include reserve accounts for roof replacement, building painting, pavement resurfacing and any other item whose deferred maintenance or replacement cost exceeds $25,000, or the inflation-adjusted amount published by the division if greater. The amount is computed from estimated remaining useful life and replacement cost.

Residential condominium associations must also complete a structural integrity reserve study at least every 10 years for each building three habitable stories or higher. The statute set a December 31, 2025 deadline for existing associations controlled by owners other than the developer, which has passed. Ask the association whether its study is on file, since the buyer must receive it or a statement that none exists.

The same section lists buildings the study rule does not reach, including those under three stories and one- to four-family dwellings with three or fewer habitable stories. A seller in a low-rise community should check the declaration to see which rules apply.

faqs.q: How long does an association have to issue an estoppel certificate?
faqs.a: Ten business days after a written or electronic request from the owner or the owner's designee, or from the mortgagee. If it is late, the association may not charge for it. Both the condominium and homeowners' association statutes use the same period.

faqs.q: What is the most an association can charge for the certificate?
faqs.a: The cap is $250 when no money is owed, with $100 more for delivery within 3 business days and up to $150 more when an amount is delinquent. The caps adjust every five years, so check the Department of Business and Professional Regulation website for current figures.

faqs.q: How long is an estoppel certificate good for?
faqs.a: Thirty days if hand delivered or sent electronically, and 35 days if mailed. If the sale or refinance has not closed in that window, ask for an amended certificate, which carries no fee and starts a new period.

faqs.q: Do I owe condo assessments after I sell?
faqs.a: You owe the assessments that came due while you owned the unit. The new owner shares liability for unpaid assessments through the transfer date, but the buyer may recover from you, so pay the estoppel balance at closing.

faqs.q: Does a Florida condo seller have to give the buyer a reserve study?
faqs.a: Yes, where one exists. Section 718.503 entitles the buyer to the most recent structural integrity reserve study or a statement that none has been completed, along with the budget and governing documents, at the seller's expense.
